Barnaby Beaver hummed a little tune as he worked on his dam, gnawing a willow branch with gusto. Suddenly, his sharp eyes spied something glinting on the riverbank, caught among the roots of an old maple tree. It was a peculiar, smooth, round object, shimmering with all the colors of the rainbow.

"Well, now!" Barnaby exclaimed, dropping his branch. "What in the wide world is that?"

He waddled closer and nudged the object with his nose. It felt cool and strange. He tried to pick it up, but it was too big for his paws alone. At last, with a mighty push, he rolled it free and set it where the sun could truly catch it. It sparkled magnificently.

Just then, Gabby Goose came waddling by, heading for her favorite patch of watercress. She stopped short when she saw the gleaming object.

"Honk! Honk!" Gabby cried, flapping her wings. "Barnaby Beaver, what have you found? It looks like a piece of the sun itself!"

Barnaby Beaver shook his head. "I don't know, Gabby. I just found it here, near the maple roots. It's very shiny."

"Shiny!" Gabby repeated, her voice growing louder. "It's more than shiny, Barnaby! It's a _Moon Shard_! I heard Old Man Owl once talk about such things, rare fragments that fall from the night sky. They say they bring good fortune to whoever finds them, and can even glow in the dark!"

"Glow in the dark?" Barnaby pondered. "I hadn't thought of that." He was a practical beaver and preferred building to dreaming.

Gabby Goose, however, was already off. She waddled furiously, honking the news to every creature she met. She told Freddy Frog that Barnaby Beaver had found a glowing Moon Shard that pulsed with magic. She told Rosie Robin that the Moon Shard was as big as a watermelon and sang sweet lullabies. By the time the story reached Sly Fox's den, it had grown tremendously.

"Barnaby Beaver," Sly Fox heard from a breathless Squirrelly Squirrel, "has found a giant, singing, _glowing_ Moon Shard that grants wishes! It's as big as Farmer Green's wheelbarrow, and it shines so brightly you can read by it at midnight!"

Sly Fox pricked up his ears. "A wish-granting Moon Shard, you say?" he murmured to himself. "This is a most interesting development." He knew that Moon Shards were as real as flying pigs; but he also knew that many of the smaller, sillier forest folk believed almost anything they heard.

"I must see this marvel for myself," Sly Fox decided. He strolled casually towards Barnaby Beaver's dam, a cunning smile playing on his lips. When he arrived, Barnaby was carefully polishing his strange, round, sparkling object with a soft leaf.

"Ah, Barnaby, my dear fellow!" Sly Fox purred. "I hear you've unearthed quite a treasure! A genuine Moon Shard, no less!"

Barnaby Beaver looked up, a bit bewildered. "It's just this shiny thing I found, Sly. I don't know what it is."

"Nonsense!" Sly Fox declared. "Of course, it's a Moon Shard! Look at how it gleams! The whole forest is talking about it. And they're all eager to see it, Barnaby. Eager to make their wishes!"

"Wishes?" Barnaby asked. "Does it grant wishes?"

"Why, certainly!" Sly Fox answered smoothly. "All Moon Shards grant wishes. But such powerful magic requires a small token of respect, you understand. A few berries, a tasty nut, perhaps even a shiny pebble, to show one's sincerity." Sly Fox grinned, already imagining the pile of treasures he could collect. "I, Sly Fox, will be the official guardian of the Moon Shard, and I shall collect these tokens for you, Barnaby, for a small fee, of course."

Before Barnaby could object, Sly Fox began to shout to the assembling crowd of curious creatures, "Come one, come all! Witness the incredible Moon Shard! Make your wishes! A small offering is required for this great privilege!"

The little animals, eager and gullible, began to line up, clutching their offerings. One by one, they approached the gleaming object, whispered their wishes, and handed their nuts and berries to Sly Fox. Barnaby Beaver watched, confused, as his simple shiny find became a center of bustling commerce.

Just as Sly Fox was raking in a particularly plump blackberry from a wide-eyed young Chipmunk, a shadow fell over the scene. Professor Hoot, the ancient and wise owl, landed silently on a branch directly above them. He peered down at the glistening object with his piercing yellow eyes.

"Hoo! Hoo!" Professor Hoot hooted softly. "What is all this commotion about?"

Sly Fox puffed out his chest. "Why, Professor Hoot, we are celebrating Barnaby Beaver's discovery of a genuine Moon Shard! And I am kindly managing the offerings for its wish-granting powers."

Professor Hoot tilted his head. He looked at the object, then at Sly Fox, then at the line of hopeful animals. "A Moon Shard?" he questioned, his voice dry. "I have studied astronomy for many years, young fox, and I can assure you that no Moon Shard has ever fallen to this forest floor. And if one did, it would not look like _that_."

He swooped down, landing lightly beside the object. He tapped it with a talon. "This, my dear creatures," Professor Hoot explained, "is merely a broken piece of a mirror, discarded by some human. Its glimmer comes from reflecting the sunlight, nothing more. It grants no wishes; it holds no magic."

A gasp went through the crowd. Barnaby Beaver looked at his shiny find, then at the collected pile of nuts and berries. Sly Fox's cunning smile vanished, replaced by a look of profound annoyance.

"A mirror?" Barnaby Beaver said, a little disappointed but also relieved. "So it's just a piece of glass?"

"Precisely," Professor Hoot confirmed. "A rather pretty piece, to be sure, but not a celestial treasure."

The small animals began to grumble and demand their offerings back. Sly Fox, looking very ruffled, had to return every berry and nut. He glared at Professor Hoot, but the wise owl merely blinked slowly.

"You see, Barnaby," Professor Hoot said, turning to the beaver, "it is always best to discover the truth for oneself, rather than to believe every story that travels through the forest. Especially when those stories grow taller with every telling." And Sly Fox, thoroughly outsmarted, could find no answer to that. He slunk away, muttering about meddling professors and gullible creatures. Barnaby, however, now knew what his shiny object truly was; and he kept it, for it still looked quite pretty catching the sun by his dam.
